CAS Monograph 16 is *From GLMs to Comprehensive Insurance Pricing: Techniques
and Challenges* (Alan Chalk, David Deacon, Montserrat Guillen and Max
Martinelli, 2025). It starts where the GLM monograph of Goldburd and others
stops. It takes the GLM as known and asks what a pricing team does next:

- how to measure a model on data that it has not seen,
- how penalized regression selects features and shrinks them,
- how step and hinge functions let a GLM bend,
- what to do with a factor that has thousands of levels,
- how to handle highly correlated features,
- how to fit a model in two stages with offsets,
- how to learn from a gradient boosting model that is better than the GLM.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.md`](glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.md).
It has the same sections, data and numbers, and it uses the R package
(`glm_fit()`, `elastic_net_fit()`, `elastic_net_cv()`, `gam_fit()`,
`booster_fit()`, `family_deviance()`). The R package calls the same Rust code as
the Python package. Its boosting adapter calls the same LightGBM (4.7.0, through
the `lightgbm` package) with the same parameters. This guide explains the
monograph in new words and calculates the numbers again. Table and section
numbers are the monograph's.

**What this guide reproduces.** The case studies of the monograph use three
data sets that are not available offline:

- the FAA aircraft registry joined to NTSB accident records,
- UK road accident counts that the authors summarized,
- a simulated auto portfolio whose rows are not published.

Thus this guide does not recompute their fitted coefficients and pseudo-R2
values. It reproduces every worked example whose inputs the monograph prints,
each with the monograph's value next to prospicio's. To show the methods on
data, the guide uses a simulated motor portfolio with a known ground truth, as
section 2.3 of the monograph does.

**The data, and how the numbers are checked.** The Python guide draws the
portfolio with the numpy generator (seed 2025). R cannot replay the numpy
draws. Thus this guide reads the same draws from
`examples/data/chalk_portfolio.csv` and `examples/data/chalk_toys.csv`, which
`examples/data/make_chalk_portfolio.py` writes with the code of the Python
guide. With the same data, every number below equals the number in the Python
guide.

CI runs every R chunk that has a text block after it
(`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R`). The chunk must print exactly that text,
which is also the text of the Python guide. The guide compares models by
pseudo-R2 rounded to three decimals, because gradient boosting libraries change
the later digits between versions and platforms. At those digits, the boosting
numbers below equal the Python numbers. To render the page, install the R
package and `lightgbm`, then run
`quarto render docs/guides/glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.qmd`.

## 1. Measuring performance (chapter 3)

### 1.1 Pseudo-R2

The monograph measures every model by one number that does not grow with the
size of the data. The number is the share of the possible improvement in
log-likelihood that the model achieves. The scale runs from the null model (the
mean for everyone) to the saturated model (each record predicted at its own
outcome). Deviance is twice the gap to the saturated model, so this share is
`1 - D_model / D_null`, the deviance explained. Table 3.1 has four records, two
claims and predictions 0.2 to 0.8:

```{r}
library(prospicio)

y <- c(0, 0, 1, 1)
mu <- c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8)
null <- rep(mean(y), length(y))

# Poisson log-likelihood without the log(y!) constant, as in section 3.1.
loglik <- function(y, mu) sum(y * log(mu) - mu)

ll_model <- loglik(y, mu)
ll_null <- loglik(y, null)
ll_sat <- sum((y * log(y) - y)[y > 0])
cat(sprintf("log-likelihood model %.3f (printed -2.734)\n", ll_model))
cat(sprintf("log-likelihood null  %.3f (printed -3.386)\n", ll_null))
cat(sprintf("log-likelihood sat.  %.3f (printed -2)\n", ll_sat))
cat(sprintf("pseudo-R2 from log-likelihoods %.3f\n", (ll_model - ll_null) / (ll_sat - ll_null)))
d_model <- family_deviance("poisson", y, mu)
d_null <- family_deviance("poisson", y, null)
cat(sprintf("pseudo-R2 from deviances       %.3f (printed 47%%)\n", 1 - d_model / d_null))
```

```text
log-likelihood model -2.734 (printed -2.734)
log-likelihood null  -3.386 (printed -3.386)
log-likelihood sat.  -2.000 (printed -2)
pseudo-R2 from log-likelihoods 0.471
pseudo-R2 from deviances       0.471 (printed 47%)
```

Both routes give the printed 47%. `family_deviance()` also takes prior
weights, for the exposure-weighted version of section 3.7.2. It multiplies the
deviance of each record by its exposure, in the model deviance and in the null
deviance.

Two more numbers in the chapter are arithmetic on printed values. In Table 3.6,
a corporation with a five-year-old aircraft has linear predictor -2.447 + 0.410
+ 5 x (-0.086) = -2.467 and frequency exp(-2.467) = 0.085. In section 3.7.4,
the factor 0.004593 / 0.004579 rebases the null model trained on folds 2 to 7
to the mean of fold 1:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("linear predictor %.3f, frequency %.3f (printed -2.467, 0.085)\n",
            -2.447 + 0.410 + 5 * -0.086, exp(-2.467)))
cat(sprintf("rebasing factor %.4f (printed 1.0031)\n", 0.004593 / 0.004579))
```

```text
linear predictor -2.467, frequency 0.085 (printed -2.467, 0.085)
rebasing factor 1.0031 (printed 1.0031)
```

### 1.2 A portfolio with a known truth, and folds from the policy number

The simulated portfolio takes the place of the monograph's case studies. It has
20,000 policies with driver age, vehicle age, region, power, a 300-level make, a
noise feature and a young-driver, high-power interaction. The true log
frequency has these parts:

- a steep young-driver effect and a rise after age 60,
- a vehicle-age effect that falls until age 6 and is flat after,
- region and power effects,
- a make effect for each of 300 makes, with make sizes that fall like a Zipf
  law,
- an extra load for young drivers of high-power cars.

`noise` has no effect. `exper` (years since the driving test) is driver age
less 17 less a small random amount. It is highly correlated with age and has no
effect of its own. The files contain the drawn features, exposures, claims and
the 300 make effects. The chunk below rebuilds the true log frequency from them
with the formula of the Python guide.

Section 3.7.3 recommends folds from the policy number, not from a random draw.
Then anyone can rebuild the folds at any time, and all records of one policy go
into one fold. Here the policy number is the row number counted from 0, and the
fold is its last digit. Folds 7 to 9 (30%) are the test data, and folds 0 to 6
are the seven cross-validation folds, as in the monograph.

```{r}
# The data files, found from the repository root (CI) or from docs/guides (Quarto).
find_data <- function(name, dir = getwd()) {
  repeat {
    path <- file.path(dir, "examples", "data", name)
    if (file.exists(path)) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (identical(parent, dir)) stop("examples/data/", name, " not found", call. = FALSE)
    dir <- parent
  }
}

pf <- utils::read.csv(find_data("chalk_portfolio.csv"), comment.char = "#")
toys <- utils::read.csv(find_data("chalk_toys.csv"), comment.char = "#")
n <- nrow(pf)
pf$region <- factor(pf$region, levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"))
pf$power <- factor(pf$power, levels = c("low", "mid", "high"))
make_effect <- toys$y[toys$example == "make_effect"]
region_effect <- c(A = 0, B = 0.15, C = -0.2, D = 0, E = 0, F = 0.3)
true_lp <- with(pf, log(0.25) + 0.9 * exp(-(age - 18) / 6) + 0.0015 * pmax(age - 60, 0)^1.5 -
  0.08 * pmin(veh_age, 6) + unname(region_effect[as.character(region)]) + make_effect[make + 1] +
  0.25 * (power == "high") + 0.6 * (power == "high" & age < 25))
pf$fold <- (seq_len(n) - 1) %% 10
train <- pf$fold < 7
cat(sprintf("%d policies, %.0f car-years, %.0f claims\n", n, sum(pf$exposure), sum(pf$claims)))
cat(sprintf("frequency %.4f; makes with under 20 policies: %d\n", sum(pf$claims) / sum(pf$exposure),
            sum(tabulate(pf$make + 1, 300) < 20)))
cat(sprintf("correlation of age and exper %.3f\n", cor(pf$age, pf$exper)))
```

```text
20000 policies, 15000 car-years, 3659 claims
frequency 0.2439; makes with under 20 policies: 166
correlation of age and exper 0.997
```

The helper below is the monograph's measure for a frequency model with
exposure. `y` are claim counts and `mu` are expected counts. The null model is
the mean frequency of the data times the exposure of each record. `cv_score()`
trains on six of the seven folds, scores the seventh, and calculates the
average. It takes any function that fits a formula on one data frame and
predicts on another. Thus it scores a GLM, a GAM and a gradient boosting model
the same way.

```{r}
pseudo_r2 <- function(y, mu, expo) {
  null <- expo * sum(y) / sum(expo)
  1 - family_deviance("poisson", y, mu) / family_deviance("poisson", y, null)
}

cv_score <- function(fit_predict, formula, folds = 0:6) {
  scores <- vapply(folds, function(k) {
    val <- pf[pf$fold == k, ]
    pseudo_r2(val$claims, fit_predict(formula, pf[train & pf$fold != k, ], val), val$exposure)
  }, double(1))
  list(mean = mean(scores), folds = scores)
}

# Python's list of formatted numbers: ['0.100', '0.200'].
py_list <- function(x, digits) {
  paste0("[", paste0("'", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x), "'", collapse = ", "), "]")
}

truth <- exp(true_lp) * pf$exposure
cat(sprintf("pseudo-R2 of the true frequencies on the test data %.3f\n",
            pseudo_r2(pf$claims[!train], truth[!train], pf$exposure[!train])))
```

```text
pseudo-R2 of the true frequencies on the test data 0.089
```

This is the lesson of section 3.7.1. A perfect model explains only a few
percent of the deviance of individual claim counts, because most of each count
is chance. The perfect model of the monograph scored 0.051 on its own
simulation. The level alone tells little. Comparisons between models on the
same data tell what is important.

### 1.3 Null, baseline and benchmark models

The null model predicts the training mean. In theory its validation pseudo-R2
is zero. In practice it is slightly negative, because the training mean is not
the mean of the validation fold (Table 3.3). Rebasing the prediction to the
mean of the fold (section 3.7.4) makes it exactly zero.

The baseline is a plain Poisson GLM with age and vehicle age as straight lines
and region and power as factors (section 3.5). The benchmark is a gradient
boosting model through `booster_fit()` (section 3.6). Here it is LightGBM with
the make as a plain number, so the trees can split on it.

The trees see region and power as the codes 0, 1, 2, ... of their levels in
alphabetical order, as `np.unique` gives them in the Python guide. The columns
are in the same order too. Thus LightGBM gets the same matrix in R and in
Python.

```{r}
pf$region_code <- as.integer(pf$region) - 1
pf$power_code <- match(as.character(pf$power), c("high", "low", "mid")) - 1
f_null <- claims ~ 1 + offset(log(exposure))
f_base <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region + power + offset(log(exposure))
f_tree <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region_code + power_code + make + noise + offset(log(exposure))
gbm_params <- list(num_leaves = 7, min_data_in_leaf = 200, num_threads = 1)

glm_fp <- function(formula, d, new) predict(glm_fit(formula, d), new)

gbm_fp <- function(formula, d, new, rounds = 150) {
  predict(booster_fit(formula, d, n_rounds = rounds, learning_rate = 0.05, params = gbm_params,
                      seed = 1), new)
}

null_cv <- cv_score(glm_fp, f_null)
cat("null model by fold     ", py_list(null_cv$folds, 4), "\n")
val <- pf[pf$fold == 0, ]
mu0 <- glm_fp(f_null, pf[train & pf$fold != 0, ], val)
rebased <- mu0 * sum(val$claims) / sum(mu0)
cat(sprintf("fold 0 rebased          %.4f\n", abs(pseudo_r2(val$claims, rebased, val$exposure))))
cat(sprintf("baseline GLM  cv        %.3f\n", cv_score(glm_fp, f_base)$mean))
cat(sprintf("benchmark GBM cv        %.3f\n", cv_score(gbm_fp, f_tree)$mean))
```

```text
null model by fold      ['-0.0000', '-0.0000', '-0.0031', '-0.0000', '-0.0009', '-0.0012', '-0.0028']
fold 0 rebased          0.0000
baseline GLM  cv        0.021
benchmark GBM cv        0.045
```

The order is the monograph's: null at zero, a GLM above it, and the boosting
model well above the GLM. The rest of the monograph shows how to close that gap
with models that a pricing team can explain.

## 2. Penalized regression (chapter 4)

### 2.1 Why fewer parameters can predict better

In the rare-car example of section 4.1, ten insurers each see one of ten cars
for a year, and one car has a claim. An unpenalized GLM at each insurer
predicts 100% or 0%. On average across the ten insurers, the prediction is
correct (10%). But each prediction is far from it, and the spread of the ten
predictions is the variance of the model. This is the population variance,
which divides by 10, as in the monograph.

```{r}
preds <- c(1, rep(0, 9))
pop_var <- mean((preds - mean(preds))^2)
cat(sprintf("mean %.2f, variance %.2f, sd %.2f (printed 0.09, 0.30)\n",
            mean(preds), pop_var, sqrt(pop_var)))
```

```text
mean 0.10, variance 0.09, sd 0.30 (printed 0.09, 0.30)
```

A model that ignores the experience of this car and predicts the 5% average for
every make has bias but no variance. Here, every insurer is closer to the truth
with it. Penalized regression trades bias for variance continuously. It
maximizes the log-likelihood less a penalty on the coefficients:

- ridge: the sum of their squares,
- lasso: the sum of their absolute values,
- elastic net: a mix of the two, with weight `alpha` on the lasso part.

`elastic_net_fit()` minimizes the glmnet objective: the mean deviance over two,
plus `lambda` times the penalty. The intercept has no penalty, and the columns
are standardized before the penalty applies. Its `lambda` and `alpha` are the
lambda and alpha of the monograph (section 4.6.3).

### 2.2 Ridge in closed form, and why features are standardized

For one feature, a normal response and no intercept, section 4.7.1 shows that
ridge divides the mean of `x * y` by the mean of `x^2` plus `lambda`. Thus it
pulls the least squares estimate towards zero. The example of section 4.7.2 has
a mean `x * y` of 10, a mean `x^2` of 5, length in metres, and `lambda` = 5. In
centimetres, the first mean is 100 times larger and the second is 10,000 times
larger. Thus the same `lambda` shrinks almost nothing:

```{r}
units <- data.frame(unit = c("metres", "centimetres"), xy = c(10, 1000), xx = c(5, 50000),
                    scale = c(1, 100))
for (i in 1:2) {
  ols <- units$xy[i] / units$xx[i]
  ridge_b <- units$xy[i] / (units$xx[i] + 5)
  cat(sprintf("%-12s least squares %.4f, ridge %.6f, frequency at 1 m %.4f\n",
              units$unit[i], ols, ridge_b, ridge_b * units$scale[i]))
}
```

```text
metres       least squares 2.0000, ridge 1.000000, frequency at 1 m 1.0000
centimetres  least squares 0.0200, ridge 0.019998, frequency at 1 m 1.9998
```

The monograph prints the centimetre estimate as 0.019 and the frequency as 1.9.
The exact values are 0.019998 and 1.9998, which round to 0.020 and 2.0. The
printed digits are truncated. The point is the same: the units, not the data,
set the effect of the penalty.

Standardizing each feature to unit standard deviation before the penalty
removes this dependence. `elastic_net_fit()` does this by default and gives
coefficients on the original scale. The same ridge on a length in metres and in
centimetres gives coefficients that differ by exactly the factor of 100. The
200 lengths are the draws of the Python guide, from `chalk_toys.csv`:

```{r}
len <- toys[toys$example == "metres", ]
b_m <- coef(elastic_net_fit(y ~ x, len, family = "gaussian", alpha = 0, lambda = 0.5))[[2]]
b_cm <- coef(elastic_net_fit(y ~ I(100 * x), len, family = "gaussian", alpha = 0, lambda = 0.5))[[2]]
cat(sprintf("metres %.6f, centimetres x 100 %.6f\n", b_m, 100 * b_cm))
```

```text
metres 1.343762, centimetres x 100 1.343762
```

### 2.3 The lasso sets coefficients to exactly zero

Section 4.7.3 gives the lasso estimate for one standardized feature. It is the
least squares estimate moved towards zero by `lambda`. It is exactly zero when
`lambda` is larger than the least squares estimate (soft-thresholding). The same
is true with the prospicio objective, where the least squares estimate is the
mean of `x * y`:

```{r}
soft <- toys[toys$example == "soft", ]
ols <- mean(soft$x * soft$y)
for (lam in c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4)) {
  b <- coef(elastic_net_fit(y ~ x, soft, family = "gaussian", alpha = 1, lambda = lam))[[2]]
  cat(sprintf("lam %.1f: lasso %.4f, soft threshold %.4f\n", lam, b, sign(ols) * max(abs(ols) - lam, 0)))
}
```

```text
lam 0.0: lasso 0.3382, soft threshold 0.3382
lam 0.1: lasso 0.2382, soft threshold 0.2382
lam 0.2: lasso 0.1382, soft threshold 0.1382
lam 0.4: lasso 0.0000, soft threshold 0.0000
```

### 2.4 Paths and choosing the penalty by cross-validation

Tables 4.1 and 4.2 fit accident frequency on the log of aircraft age alone.
They show how the coefficient shrinks as the penalty increases: smoothly
towards zero for ridge, and to exactly zero for the lasso. The chunk below does
the same on the portfolio, with log driver age. For a Poisson model, the sum of
the records at each set of feature values gives the same fit (section 8.3 also
says this). Thus the age-only models below use 63 ages times 10 folds, not
20,000 policies.

`elastic_net_fit()` with `lambda = NULL` gives the default glmnet path. The
first `lambda` of this path is the smallest that sets every coefficient to
zero:

```{r}
cells <- aggregate(cbind(claims, exposure) ~ age + fold, pf, sum)
cells <- cells[order(cells$age * 10 + cells$fold), ]
cells$log_age <- log(cells$age)
cells_tr <- cells[cells$fold < 7, ]
f_logage <- claims ~ log_age + offset(log(exposure))
top <- elastic_net_fit(f_logage, cells_tr, alpha = 1)@lambda[1]
for (a in c(0, 1)) {
  scale <- if (a == 0) 100 else 1
  lams <- scale * top * c(1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.03, 0.01, 0)
  path <- elastic_net_fit(f_logage, cells_tr, alpha = a, lambda = lams)
  cat(sprintf("%-5s log-age coefficient:", if (a == 0) "ridge" else "lasso"),
      py_list(path@coefficients["log_age", ], 3), "\n")
}
```

```text
ridge log-age coefficient: ['-0.023', '-0.067', '-0.153', '-0.275', '-0.354', '-0.413']
lasso log-age coefficient: ['0.000', '-0.292', '-0.373', '-0.401', '-0.409', '-0.413']
```

The last value of each row is the unpenalized GLM. Section 4.3 chooses `lambda`
as follows:

1. Fit the full path on six folds.
2. Score it on the seventh fold.
3. Calculate the average over the seven choices of validation fold.

`elastic_net_cv()` does these steps (as `cv.glmnet()` in glmnet), here with
`foldid` the policy-number folds. It gives the `lambda` with the best mean
validation deviance. For the one-standard-error rule of section 4.6.5, it also
gives the largest `lambda` within one standard error of that value. Below, the
positions on the path start at 0, as in the Python guide:

```{r}
lams <- elastic_net_fit(f_logage, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, nlambda = 30, lambda_min_ratio = 1e-3)@lambda
path_cv <- elastic_net_cv(f_logage, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, lambda = lams, foldid = cells_tr$fold + 1)
cat(sprintf("lam_min at position %d of 30, lam_1se at position %d\n",
            which(lams == path_cv$lambda_min) - 1, which(lams == path_cv$lambda_1se) - 1))
```

```text
lam_min at position 29 of 30, lam_1se at position 3
```

### 2.5 The relaxed lasso

The lasso selects features and also shrinks them. The relaxed lasso of section
4.5 separates the two steps. It keeps the features that the lasso selected and
fits them again with less penalty or no penalty (hard thresholding). In
prospicio, the second step is a `glm_fit()` on the selected columns. Section
3.2 below uses it.

## 3. Nonlinear effects (chapter 5)

### 3.1 Step and hinge functions, from the printed coefficients

A step function is 1 at or above a threshold and 0 below it. A hinge is zero
below its knot and increases by one per unit above it: `max(0, x - knot)`. With
a step at age 30, the GLM of section 5.2 is
`log frequency = -5.2815 - 1.4689 x step_30`. With steps at 5, 15 and 30, the
monograph prints four frequencies. The chunk calculates them again from the
printed coefficients:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("one step: %.5f, relativity %.4f (printed 0.00509, 0.2302)\n", exp(-5.2815), exp(-1.4689)))
three <- exp(cumsum(c(-4.8292, -0.6881, -0.5711, -0.6237)))
printed <- c(0.00783, 0.00394, 0.00222, 0.00119)
cat("three steps:", py_list(three, 5), "printed [0.00783, 0.00394, 0.00222, 0.00119]\n")
cat("printed / recomputed:", py_list(printed / three, 3), "\n")
```

```text
one step: 0.00508, relativity 0.2302 (printed 0.00509, 0.2302)
three steps: ['0.00799', '0.00402', '0.00227', '0.00122'] printed [0.00783, 0.00394, 0.00222, 0.00119]
printed / recomputed: ['0.980', '0.981', '0.978', '0.979']
```

The relativity of the single step matches. Its base frequency differs in the
last digit: exp(-5.2815) is 0.005082, which rounds to 0.00508, not to the
printed 0.00509. An intercept of -5.2809 or more gives the printed value.

The three-step frequencies do not match. Each printed value is about 2% below
the value from the printed coefficients, by almost the same factor in all four
bands. A common factor points at the intercept, not at the slopes. An intercept
near -4.85, not -4.8292, gives the printed frequencies. The ratios between bands
agree with the printed slopes in both cases. Without the data, we cannot say
which printed number is wrong.

Table 5.7 codes an ordinal feature (pilot quality, five levels) as five
cumulative steps and multiplies the exponentiated coefficients:

```{r}
cat("cumulative relativities:", py_list(exp(cumsum(c(0, 0.515, 0, 0.211, 0.206))), 3), "\n")
```

```text
cumulative relativities: ['1.000', '1.674', '1.674', '2.067', '2.540']
```

The printed cumulative row is 1, 1.673, 1.673, 2.06, 2.539, and Table 5.8 gives
the fourth value as 2.07. The exact product is 2.067, so Table 5.7 truncates and
Table 5.8 rounds.

### 3.2 Many steps or hinges, and the lasso picks

Section 5.2 does not select knots by eye. It gives the lasso one step function
at each age and lets cross-validation decide how many steps stay. Section 5.6
uses 25 equally spaced steps or hinges for each feature. The chunk below uses
the ages of the portfolio (aggregated as above), with a step every three years
from 20 to 77:

```{r}
knots <- seq(20, 77, by = 3)
step_names <- paste0("age_stp_", knots)
add_steps <- function(d, at) {
  for (a in at) d[[paste0("age_stp_", a)]] <- as.numeric(d$age >= a)
  d
}
cells <- add_steps(cells, knots)
cells_tr <- cells[cells$fold < 7, ]
f_steps <- reformulate(c(step_names, "offset(log(exposure))"), "claims")
lams <- elastic_net_fit(f_steps, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, nlambda = 25, lambda_min_ratio = 1e-3)@lambda
cvp <- elastic_net_cv(f_steps, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, lambda = lams, foldid = cells_tr$fold + 1)
i_min <- which(lams == cvp$lambda_min)
i_1se <- which(lams == cvp$lambda_1se)
kept <- knots[cvp$fit@coefficients[step_names, i_min] != 0]
cat(sprintf("%d steps offered, %d kept at lam_min, %d at lam_1se\n",
            length(knots), cvp$fit@df[i_min], cvp$fit@df[i_1se]))
cat("kept:", paste0("[", paste(kept, collapse = ", "), "]"), "\n")
```

```text
20 steps offered, 8 kept at lam_min, 5 at lam_1se
kept: [20, 23, 26, 29, 32, 62, 65, 77]
```

The next chunk compares three fits with the truth by age. The true frequency at
an age is the exposure-weighted average of the true frequencies of the policies
at that age. The three fits are:

- the lasso at `lambda_min`,
- the relaxed lasso: the kept steps fitted again by an unpenalized `glm_fit()`
  (section 4.5),
- a P-spline GAM (`gam_fit()`), the smoothing model that the monograph uses for
  its spatial second stage in chapter 8.

```{r}
grid <- add_steps(data.frame(age = 18:80, exposure = 1), knots)
true_by_age <- tapply(truth, pf$age, sum) / tapply(pf$exposure, pf$age, sum)
lasso_curve <- predict(cvp$fit, grid, lambda = cvp$lambda_min)
f_kept <- reformulate(c(paste0("age_stp_", kept), "offset(log(exposure))"), "claims")
relaxed_curve <- predict(glm_fit(f_kept, cells_tr), grid)
gam_age <- gam_fit(claims ~ age + offset(log(exposure)), cells_tr, smooths = "age", n_basis = 12)
gam_curve <- predict(gam_age, grid)
for (a in c(18, 20, 23, 26, 35, 50, 65, 80)) {
  i <- a - 17
  cat(sprintf("age %d: truth %.3f  lasso %.3f  relaxed %.3f  GAM %.3f\n",
              a, true_by_age[[i]], lasso_curve[i], relaxed_curve[i], gam_curve[i]))
}
cat(sprintf("GAM effective degrees of freedom %.1f\n", gam_age@edf))
```

```text
age 18: truth 0.565  lasso 0.531  relaxed 0.553  GAM 0.530
age 20: truth 0.481  lasso 0.408  relaxed 0.415  GAM 0.449
age 23: truth 0.363  lasso 0.304  relaxed 0.310  GAM 0.355
age 26: truth 0.264  lasso 0.256  relaxed 0.260  GAM 0.290
age 35: truth 0.216  lasso 0.207  relaxed 0.200  GAM 0.206
age 50: truth 0.207  lasso 0.207  relaxed 0.200  GAM 0.195
age 65: truth 0.215  lasso 0.236  relaxed 0.239  GAM 0.228
age 80: truth 0.256  lasso 0.239  relaxed 0.253  GAM 0.249
GAM effective degrees of freedom 5.7
```

All three fits find the young-driver slope and the rise after 60 with no
information about where they are. The lasso shrinkage pulls the extremes
towards the middle, the effect that section 5.2 sees above aircraft age 20. The
relaxed fit removes part of this effect. The monograph prefers steps and hinges
because the result is a short rating table. A GAM gives a smooth curve, which
you tabulate afterwards.

Section 5.8.1 links steps to the fused lasso by a change of coordinates. A step
at each level is the same model as a dummy at each level. The coefficient of
each step is the difference between neighbouring dummies. Thus a lasso penalty
on steps is a penalty on the jumps between neighbours.

### 3.3 Monotone effects

Section 5.7.2 makes an ordinal effect monotone with non-negative step
coefficients. A GAM can also set the shape directly: `bs = "mpd"` is a monotone
decreasing P-spline (from scam). The chunk fits it to vehicle age, whose true
effect falls until age 6 and is flat after:

```{r}
veh <- aggregate(cbind(claims, exposure) ~ veh_age + fold, pf, sum)
mono <- gam_fit(claims ~ veh_age + offset(log(exposure)), veh[veh$fold < 7, ], smooths = "veh_age",
                n_basis = 8, bs = "mpd")
curve <- predict(mono, data.frame(veh_age = 0:20, exposure = 1))
show <- c(0, 2, 4, 6, 10, 15, 20)
cat("fitted relativity to age 0:", py_list((curve / curve[1])[show + 1], 2), "\n")
cat("true relativity:           ", py_list(exp(-0.08 * pmin(show, 6)), 2), "\n")
```

```text
fitted relativity to age 0: ['1.00', '0.89', '0.80', '0.75', '0.70', '0.64', '0.61']
true relativity:            ['1.00', '0.85', '0.73', '0.62', '0.62', '0.62', '0.62']
```

The monotone fit bends more gradually than the true hinge. It continues to fall
a little after age 6, where the truth is flat, but it cannot turn back up. The
monograph gives a warning: a constraint hides a reversal if the data has one.
Use a constraint where the shape is known (claim history, deductibles), not to
make a factor look tidy.

## 4. High cardinality categorical variables (chapter 6)

### 4.1 Target encoding, and keeping it out of its own fold

A factor with thousands of levels (aircraft make, city, zip code) causes
problems as dummies in a GLM. It uses much memory and gives unstable estimates
for the thin levels. The main tool of chapter 6 is target encoding. It replaces
each level by one number: its actual-to-expected ratio, shrunk towards 1 by a
credibility factor `z = n / (n + K)`, where `n` is the exposure of the level.
The log of that number is then a feature.

Encoding a level from its own records leaks the target into the feature
(section 6.3). Thus a record in fold `k` gets its encoding only from the other
folds. Table 6.1 has one make with six aircraft in three folds:

```{r}
te_fold <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)
te_acc <- c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1)
for (k in 1:3) {
  other <- te_fold != k
  cat(sprintf("fold %d: accidents elsewhere %.0f on %d aircraft, encoding %.2f\n",
              k, sum(te_acc[other]), sum(other), mean(te_acc[other])))
}
cat("printed: 0.75, 0.50, 0.25\n")
```

```text
fold 1: accidents elsewhere 3 on 4 aircraft, encoding 0.75
fold 2: accidents elsewhere 2 on 4 aircraft, encoding 0.50
fold 3: accidents elsewhere 1 on 4 aircraft, encoding 0.25
printed: 0.75, 0.50, 0.25
```

### 4.2 The credibility constant, and the printed encodings

Section 6.6 estimates `K` as a ratio of two variances. The numerator is the
within-make variance: the accident count of one aircraft-year, Bernoulli at the
mean rate 0.004584. The denominator is the between-make variance, which the
monograph estimates from mean residuals of large makes as 7.038492e-6. Table
6.5 lists encoded makes at `K` = 1,024, the value that the monograph uses at the
end. The chunk calculates these values again from the printed inputs:

```{r}
p <- 0.004584
within <- p * (1 - p)
K_est <- within / 7.038492e-6
cat(sprintf("within variance %.9f (printed 0.004562987), K %.0f (printed 648), credibility at 1,000 aircraft-years %.2f (printed 0.61)\n",
            within, K_est, 1000 / (1000 + 648)))
table_6_5 <- data.frame(
  make = c("DJI", "TEXTRON AVIATION INC", "MARLIN JOHN E", "STUMP GREAT LAKES"),
  expo = c(11900, 5483, 13, 12), ave = c(0, 0.24356, 186.59373, 223.74936),
  z_printed = c("0.9208", "0.8426", "0.0122", "0.0116"), te_printed = c(0.079, 0.363, 3.266, 3.579)
)
for (i in 1:4) {
  r <- table_6_5[i, ]
  z <- r$expo / (r$expo + 1024)
  zp <- as.numeric(r$z_printed)
  cat(sprintf("%-21s z %.4f (printed %s)  encoding %.3f, from the printed z %.3f (printed %s)\n",
              r$make, z, r$z_printed, 1 - z + z * r$ave, 1 - zp + zp * r$ave, format(r$te_printed)))
}
```

```text
within variance 0.004562987 (printed 0.004562987), K 648 (printed 648), credibility at 1,000 aircraft-years 0.61 (printed 0.61)
DJI                   z 0.9208 (printed 0.9208)  encoding 0.079, from the printed z 0.079 (printed 0.079)
TEXTRON AVIATION INC  z 0.8426 (printed 0.8426)  encoding 0.363, from the printed z 0.363 (printed 0.363)
MARLIN JOHN E         z 0.0125 (printed 0.0122)  encoding 3.327, from the printed z 3.264 (printed 3.266)
STUMP GREAT LAKES     z 0.0116 (printed 0.0116)  encoding 3.580, from the printed z 3.584 (printed 3.579)
```

DJI and Textron match. For the two one-claim makes, the exposure column shows a
whole number of aircraft-years. The printed credibility of Marlin (0.0122)
implies about 12.65 aircraft-years, not 13. Thus the column is rounded, and the
encoding from the printed `z` is 3.264. Stump Great Lakes gives 3.580 against
3.579 (3.584 from its rounded printed `z`), and the difference also comes from
a rounded exposure.

In section 6.7.1, the worked sentence for Stump multiplies `z` by 222.22, but
Table 6.5 has an AvE ratio of 223.75. The value 223.75 gives the printed 3.58,
so 222.22 is an error in the text. The caption of the table also describes the
AvE ratio upside down, as predicted over actual. Its values are actual over
expected.

Two smaller checks come from the same chapter. The first is the Bell helicopter
example of section 6.7.2. It encodes against the overall mean (16 per thousand
against 4) and against the GLM prediction for helicopters (16 against 20). The
second is the logistic blending of the software in section 6.7.6, at a level
with no data. That level should get no credibility, but it gets some:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("Bell: %.2f against the mean, %.2f against the GLM (printed 4 and 0.80)\n", 16 / 4, 16 / 20))
for (smoothing in c(100, 500)) {
  cat(sprintf("logistic credibility at n = 0, inflection 500, smoothing %d: %.3f\n",
              smoothing, 1 / (1 + exp((500 - 0) / smoothing))))
}
```

```text
Bell: 4.00 against the mean, 0.80 against the GLM (printed 4 and 0.80)
logistic credibility at n = 0, inflection 500, smoothing 100: 0.007
logistic credibility at n = 0, inflection 500, smoothing 500: 0.269
```

The second value is the "about 25%" of section 6.7.6: credibility for a level
with no data.

### 4.3 Ridge regression on dummies is credibility

Section 6.8.1 shows why target encoding is natural. Take ridge regression on
the dummies of one factor, with a normal response, the response centred and no
intercept. It gives each level the coefficient
`n_k (mean_k - mean) / (n_k + lambda)`, a credibility-weighted deviation from
the overall mean. prospicio minimizes the mean squared error over two, plus
`lambda` over two times the sum of squares. With this objective, the `lambda`
of the monograph is the prospicio `lambda` times the number of records.

A formula with `0 +` has no intercept, so `elastic_net_fit()` fits exactly that
model. The 456 responses are the draws of the Python guide:

```{r}
lvl <- toys[toys$example == "dummies", ]
sizes <- c(1, 5, 50, 400)
lvl$yc <- lvl$y - mean(lvl$y)
lvl$level <- factor(lvl$x, levels = 0:3, labels = paste0("level", 0:3))
lam <- 0.1
fit <- elastic_net_fit(yc ~ 0 + level, lvl, family = "gaussian", alpha = 0, lambda = lam,
                       standardize = FALSE)
K <- lam * nrow(lvl)
for (j in 1:4) {
  z <- sizes[j] / (sizes[j] + K)
  cat(sprintf("level %d (%3d records): ridge %+.4f, z x deviation %+.4f  (z = %.3f)\n",
              j - 1, sizes[j], coef(fit)[[j]], z * mean(lvl$yc[lvl$x == j - 1]), z))
}
```

```text
level 0 (  1 records): ridge +0.0456, z x deviation +0.0456  (z = 0.021)
level 1 (  5 records): ridge -0.0470, z x deviation -0.0470  (z = 0.099)
level 2 ( 50 records): ridge +0.2407, z x deviation +0.2407  (z = 0.523)
level 3 (400 records): ridge -0.0511, z x deviation -0.0511  (z = 0.898)
```

The penalty does the work of the Buhlmann `K`, with one difference that the
monograph stresses. Credibility theory estimates `K` from variance components,
but penalized regression chooses it by cross-validation.

### 4.4 Target encoding the portfolio's 300 makes

On the portfolio, the make encoding follows section 6.7.2. The expected count
of each policy is the prediction of a first GLM without make. This GLM is
cross-fitted, so no model predicts a record that it saw in training. The
encoding of each make is its shrunk actual-to-expected ratio. The log encoding
then goes into a second-stage GLM with the first-GLM prediction as offset, as in
section 6.9. For each `K` in a grid, the seven-fold cross-validation repeats the
full procedure inside each fold:

```{r}
expected <- numeric(n)
for (j in 0:6) {
  fit_j <- glm_fit(f_base, pf[train & pf$fold != j, ])
  expected[pf$fold == j] <- predict(fit_j, pf[pf$fold == j, ])
}
expected[!train] <- predict(glm_fit(f_base, pf[train, ]), pf[!train, ])

# Sums by make, one per make 0 to 299.
by_make <- function(rows, v) {
  out <- numeric(300)
  s <- rowsum(v[rows], pf$make[rows])
  out[as.integer(rownames(s)) + 1] <- s
  out
}

# Each make's shrunk actual-to-expected ratio from the rows in `source`.
encode <- function(source, K) {
  actual <- by_make(source, pf$claims)
  exp_ <- by_make(source, expected)
  z <- by_make(source, pf$exposure) / (by_make(source, pf$exposure) + K)
  1 - z + z * ifelse(exp_ > 0, actual / exp_, 1)
}

# Per policy: a training row in fold j is encoded from the training folds other than j
# (and other than the held-out fold); every other row from all training folds but the held-out one.
make_feature <- function(K, held_out = -1) {
  te <- encode(train & pf$fold != held_out, K)[pf$make + 1]
  for (j in setdiff(0:6, held_out)) {
    in_j <- pf$fold == j
    te[in_j] <- encode(train & pf$fold != j & pf$fold != held_out, K)[pf$make[in_j] + 1]
  }
  log(te)
}

stage1 <- lapply(0:6, function(k) predict(glm_fit(f_base, pf[train & pf$fold != k, ]), pf))
cat(sprintf("%6s %13s %12s\n", "K", "cv pseudo-R2", "coefficient"))
for (K in c(16, 64, 256, 1024, 4096)) {
  res <- vapply(0:6, function(k) {
    d2 <- data.frame(claims = pf$claims, log_te = make_feature(K, k), s1 = stage1[[k + 1]])
    fit2 <- glm_fit(claims ~ log_te + offset(log(s1)), d2[train & pf$fold != k, ])
    val <- pf$fold == k
    c(pseudo_r2(pf$claims[val], predict(fit2, d2[val, ]), pf$exposure[val]), coef(fit2)[["log_te"]])
  }, double(2))
  cat(sprintf("%6d %13.3f %12.2f\n", K, mean(res[1, ]), mean(res[2, ])))
}
```

```text
     K  cv pseudo-R2  coefficient
    16         0.040         0.82
    64         0.041         1.08
   256         0.039         1.41
  1024         0.037         2.24
  4096         0.035         4.98
```

The baseline GLM scored 0.021 without make, and the encoded make approximately
doubles that. As in Figure 6.1 of the monograph, the score is flat over a wide
range of `K`, with the best value near 64. The coefficient increases with `K`,
as in Figure 6.2. A heavily shrunk encoding needs a coefficient above 1 to
restore the spread, and a coefficient near 1 means that the credibility was
approximately correct.

Here the best score and a coefficient near 1 occur at the same `K`. Section 6.6
expects this when the encoding is correct. The rest of the guide uses `K` = 64.

A generalized linear mixed model (section 6.5) treats make as a random effect
and shrinks it the same way. Section 6.8.2 gives the Bayesian view of ridge,
which is `bayes_glm_fit()` with normal priors.
